Find $\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}$ for the right-opening parabola shown above.
examples.worked_solution:
The diagram shows that the parabola has its vertex at $O,$ and passes through the point $(3,-2).$

The standard equation of a left- or right-opening parabola whose vertex is at $(0,0)$ is given by

$$
y^2 = 4px.
$$

Substituting $x = 3$ and $y = -2$ into the equation above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)^{2} & =4p(3) \\ 4 & =12p \\ p & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the equation of our parabola is 

$$
y^2 = \dfrac{4}{3}x.
$$

Finally, to calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{4}{3}x) \\ 2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{4}{3} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2}{3y}\end{aligned}
$$

Find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ for the ellipse shown above.
feedback.worked_solution:
Since our ellipse is centered at the origin and has semiaxes $5$ and $3,$ its equation is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1\,⟹\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}=1.
$$

Now, to calculate $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x},$ we use implicit differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{25})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{y}^{2}}{9}) & =0 \\ \frac{2x}{25}+\frac{2y}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =0 \\ \frac{2y}{9}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{2x}{25} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{9x}{25y}\end{aligned}
$$
